Every inbound enquiry is scored before anyone spends time on it. We have found that the
scoring matters more than the speed of the reply, so take the time to do it properly and
do not skip a dimension because it feels obvious in the moment.

Score each enquiry on five dimensions, one to five, and record the score alongside the
enquiry:

  Persuadability-Index — how open the contact is to changing an existing arrangement
  Reach-Confidence — how sure we are that this contact can actually authorise the change
  Timing-Fit — whether their renewal or review window is close enough to matter
  Margin-Headroom — how much room the deal leaves once delivery cost is taken out
  Switch-Cost — what it would cost them to move away from what they use today

An enquiry advances only at a combined score of eighteen or above. Below that it goes back
to the queue and is scored again the following month, because circumstances change and a
low score today is not a permanent verdict.

Evidence decays, and how fast it decays depends on where it came from. Classify every
supporting signal before you rely on it:

  | Evidence class    | Stays valid for |
  |-------------------|-----------------|
  | Observed-Signal   | 30 days         |
  | Inferred-Signal   | 10 days         |
  | Reported-Signal   | 5 days          |

Never advance an enquiry on a Reported-Signal alone. If the only thing supporting a high
Timing-Fit score is something the contact told us in passing, treat the score as
provisional and say so in the record.

The point of all this is that we would rather turn down work early than discover halfway
through a delivery that the arrangement never made sense. When in doubt, the more
conservative reading of the evidence is the right one.
